title: Urgency Is Not an Argument
author: David James
summary: David James critiques Anthony Seldon and Tim Bunting's pamphlet Britain's Greatest Education Opportunity Ever, which urges English schools to embrace AI immediately. He begins with style, arguing that the pamphlet's reliance on clichés and panic register substitutes tone for argument. On substance, he challenges the proposed AI taskforce modelled on the Covid vaccine effort as conflating a real crisis with an undefined one. He also questions the evidence, noting that a Chinese study of 26,000 pupils is read as causal when the comparison group was simply non-users, and that Estonia's AI Leap programme has no results yet. He objects to the idea that Ofsted should downgrade schools judged not AI-ready, to the absence of any UK budget figure, and to examples drawn largely from Wellington College, the authors' own institution. His conclusion is that schools need measured responses tested against hard evidence rather than short-termist solutionism.
points: The pamphlet's alarmist, cliché-heavy language substitutes tone for argument, and the media rarely scrutinise AI claims.
Comparing AI to the Covid vaccine taskforce conflates a recognised crisis with an undefined one and does not explain why a temporary central unit would succeed.
Key evidence is weak: a Chinese study treats non-users as a natural control group, and Estonia's programme has not yet produced results.
Having Ofsted downgrade schools that are not AI-ready would punish schools with other priorities or fewer resources, and no UK costings are offered.
Examples of good practice are drawn from a narrow pool, including the authors' own school, so the case needs wider, more objective corroboration.
quotes: Too many people too quickly respond to the tone, rather than the ideas themselves.

Just writing in a register of panic does not convey energy in itself, and nor should it disguise the serious questions we should ask when yet another set of ideas are unveiled that demand sweeping changes to schools.
it conflates one recognised and real crisis with another which is undefined, both in its nature and its threat to life (despite what the various tech bros have said).
For instance, a Chinese study of 26,000 pupils is read as showing that AI use caused a 20 per cent drop in exam scores, when the ‘natural control group’ was simply the pupils who chose not to use it.

The most contentious recommendation is that Ofsted should downgrade schools that are not sufficiently AI-ready. This seems designed to punish those schools that either have different priorities from promoting AI in the classroom, or simply do not have the trained staff, and resources, to do so.
The ten recommendations and five scenarios are offered without a single UK budget figure attached.
But we need responses that are more measured and less alarmist, and which are tested against hard evidence.
